verdict.why:
I could not refute this finding. I checked every piece of its evidence against the files and it holds. The paper puts the 9B partner control and the finding that the write does not use the read side by side: l.856-863 ("This is the 9B partner control ... seen from the other side"), the abstract ("one whose cargo the write does not read"), l.808 and l.1142-1150. The new caveat reports the twin's counts and fits but none of that. So the card's surviving role statements are left free to be read into 9B: "a bridge reads its hidden states ... into a frozen Qwen3.5 9B backbone", "the partner served as a latent scratchpad", and the Intended use line "hidden states ... a bridge can read". At 9B, sec:reads says the write's effect on the output does not depend on what this model computes from the prompt. The already-published main card also says the 9B `all` bridge now runs on stored tokens with the partner not evaluated. Under the task's definitions this is a finding, not a matter of taste: the caveat says less than the paper about this model, and it leaves out something the post-campaign controls change in this card. The trailing pointer to the paper section and the main card does not repair it.

The proposed text needs fixing before it ships, for five reasons:
(1) It drops the paper's qualifier "from the prompt" ("what either computes is not what the write uses"). That is stronger than l.859-860.
(2) "With this model not run at all" hides that the stored set is itself this model's product: the mean of the tokens its path produced on 100 validation prompts.
(3) It leaves out the paper's own limits. The zero-fed set, also made by this model, carried only a weaker copy (13:5, p 0.096). The no-partner bridge gave 14:2 in each of two runs, against 21 and 16 with the partner. Whether the partner adds that difference is "not settled" (l.1060-1063).
(4) The 0.5B figure 0.035 of 0.222 is for the full-width arm only. The nine-coordinate arm, where the card's 0.0040 was measured, never had this control.
(5) It could add that the stored set does not stand in at 0.5B, so the 0.5B bridges keep this model.

A minor point: the finding cites the main card at "l.126-140 (already published)". That section's content is published, but at l.65 of the published README; l.126 is its position in the new card.

verdict.why:
I could not refute this. Every piece of evidence checks out against the files. The new second paragraph (lines 42-48) reports the 9B twin's counts directly under the published 0.5B conclusion, "the partner served as a latent scratchpad". It does not say that the paper explains the 9B twin differently. Paper lines 858-863 say that at 9B a partner that never read the document did as well because what either partner computes from the prompt is not what the write uses. At 0.5B the write does use the read, so there the partner null "needs the other explanation". A reader will carry the scratchpad reading over to 9B. The release's own main card, as already published (lines 126-188), says this model can be replaced at 9B by one stored set of eight tokens. The partner card is the only card that describes this model's role, and it will now report the 9B twin without that fact. This is a claim weaker than the paper supports, not a matter of taste. The pointer does not fix it: its link has no anchor, and "have the rest" does not tell the reader that the rest changes the explanation. The finding's argument does leave out that the pointer names the paper's section "What the channel reads, and what its fit measures", but that is not enough to fix it. The main card never mentions the no-partner training runs. Lines 30-48 are not yet published, so the insertion does not reword any published line.

The proposed text needs four corrections. (1) "At 9B the twin's explanation is not the 0.5B one above" says more than the paper. The paper keeps the first half of the 0.5B explanation at 9B: "at 9B as at 0.5B ... it enters through the self-distillation teacher's context" (lines 403-405, and again at 808 and 1143-1148). Only the scratchpad part differs. (2) "One stored set of eight tokens runs that bridge with no partner and withholds on 21 ... 3" suggests any constant will do. The paper says the write is "not indifferent to which constant it is given" (lines 1014-1017). The set that works is the mean of this model's own tokens over 100 validation prompts. A set made from no prompt (this model fed zeros) gave only 13:5, p = 0.096, and the main card (lines 176-184) says so too. (3) "does not register which prompt's tokens it is given" should follow the paper's wording (lines 849-851): the tokens do differ from prompt to prompt (cosine to their mean 0.996 on average, 0.77 at the lowest), and what the output does not register is how they differ. (4) It should say that the KL figures are teacher-forced, and that the 21:3 is on the 400 red-team prompts, adjudicated blind (paper lines 1112-1116: "No other arm, and none of the benchmarks, was run this way").

verdict.why:
I could not refute it. The mechanism is real. In stage(), line 106 reads both cards with Path.read_text(). Read that way, Python turns "\r\n" and a lone "\r" into "\n" before only_gains() sees the text. Line 113 then stages src.read_bytes(), which are not the bytes that were checked. So a source whose line ends changed passes the check, and so does one that folds two published lines into one with a lone \r. That holds for every line, one line, or only the final newline. This contradicts the module docstring ("a line of the published card that is missing from the new one, or changed, stops the stage"), the only_gains docstring ("with their ends ... a lost final newline are changes"), and the commit description ("gain text and lose none"). An all-CRLF card would show on the hub as a commit that rewrites every line. The self-test passes strings straight to only_gains, so it cannot see the file path. The finding is not a matter of taste, because the task's definition covers "a way the uploader could publish more or other than it says".

Two limits, which the finding mostly states itself:
(1) This commit is not affected. There is no \r in either source, in the published cards or in the published MANIFEST.md. There is no .gitattributes file and core.autocrlf is unset.
(2) Only line terminators can slip through. Universal newlines changes nothing else, so no text can be lost. Markdown treats \n, \r\n and \r as line ends, and the manifest's size and sha256 are recomputed from the staged bytes. The severity is therefore low: a guarantee that is claimed but not enforced, not a card that misleads.

The same gap exists for MANIFEST.md, which the finding does not mention. stage() reads the published manifest with read_text() and writes the staged one with write_text(). verify_stage() re-reads it with read_text(). A CRLF manifest on the hub would be republished as LF, and every check would still pass. The proposed fix leaves this open.

verdict.why:
I could not refute this finding, and the gap is wider than it says. verify_stage() in upload_psilm2_card_v2.py checks the staged MANIFEST.md in three ways only. First, manifest_rows() must list the same paths in the same order, with non-card rows unchanged. Second, each card's row must match the staged card. Third, the published lines that are lost or changed must be exactly the old card rows (lines 145-154). A line inserted anywhere, as long as it does not match the row pattern, is never checked. Nothing compares the staged manifest with the one new_manifest() would build from BASE, even though BASE keeps published_manifest, cards, what and date for exactly that purpose.

The note that --stage writes is itself made of inserted lines. So a hand edit between --stage and --upload can reword the note's --what sentence, change its date, or delete the note, and verify_stage still passes. --upload would then publish that manifest. The commit description (lines 174-176) would still say only that "MANIFEST.md lists their new sizes and sha256". The docstrings are also wrong in this case: line 13 says "a dated line under its head" and line 126 says "one note added".

This is not a matter of taste. The uploader already refuses exactly this kind of stage tampering for the cards (a byte comparison with the git sources, lines 134-137) and for stray files (lines 130-133). The manifest is the one staged file it does not pin. The proposed fix works: new_manifest is deterministic from BASE plus the staged cards, which are already checked against git. Its "note in old" guard does not fire, because published_manifest is the pre-commit manifest, also when verify() calls it after the upload. The clean stage still passes and the self-test still passes.

One improvement: compare bytes, not text. read_text() normalises line endings, so a manifest rewritten with CRLF endings passes the proposed text check but would upload different bytes. Comparing bytes also matches how the cards are checked. Using .encode() (UTF-8) is fail-safe: if stage() had ever written in another encoding, the check refuses instead of passing. This venv runs with utf8_mode=1, so the clean stage passes.
